title: Colonial Brazil
titleline: Colonial Brazil - The History Web
para1: Colonial Brazil. Colonial Brazil began with a wide turn at sea: in 1500, Pedro Alvares Cabral, commanding an imposing armada bound for India on sailing directions drawn up by da Gama himself, bore so far to the west that on April 22 he sighted the mainland of South America. The Treaty of Tordesillas had divided the New World between Spanish and Portuguese claims, and the region Cabral sighted lay well within the Portuguese zone; the crown promptly claimed it. Whether the landfall was pure accident or quietly planned by the ever-secretive Portuguese, Cabral stayed eight days at Baia Cabralia, where he met Amerindians, before sailing on. Brazil matters because Portugal's accidental landfall grew into the largest colony of South America - a land that would be, at one time or another, the world's leading producer of sugar, diamonds, and tobacco.
para2: Colonized from the 1530s, Brazil was organized in 1533 into fifteen hereditary captaincies, or fiefs, each extending about fifty leagues along the coast; the captain-generals wielded extensive rights and privileges, but only two of the captaincies were ultimately successful - Sao Vicente, in present Sao Paulo state, and Pernambuco in the northeast. Pernambuco, centered on the town of Olinda, became under its donatario Duarte Coelho Pereira a great sugar-producing region, offering the first example of a profitable agrarian economy in the colony; by the mid-16th century the two successful captaincies had a combined population of only about 5,000. From those modest beginnings - sugar estates worked increasingly by enslaved Africans, coastal towns, and frontier expeditions - would grow the continent's Portuguese-speaking giant. The Crown appointed a governor in 1549 to bring order to the colony, which became an official viceroyalty later divided in two, with Salvador the capital of the north and Rio de Janeiro of the south. Sugar's labor demands drove the slave trade: after the enslaving of Amerindians was prohibited from 1570, most enslaved workers came by ship from Africa, particularly Portuguese Angola - 150,000 during sugar's peak from 1600 to 1625 alone - and the result was a great mixing of Europeans, Amerindians, and Africans, more so than in any other Portuguese colony.

title: Gran Colombia
titleline: Gran Colombia - The History Web
para1: Gran Colombia. Gran Colombia was the republic formed in the heat of the independence wars from the territories of the Viceroyalty of New Granada - roughly the modern nations of Colombia, Panama, Venezuela, and Ecuador. In 1819, in the context of their war for independence, the patriots set up a regular government at a congress in Angostura - now Ciudad Bolivar, Venezuela - and the republic was definitely organized at the Congress of Cucuta on August 30, 1821 - a conglomerate of recently freed countries formerly part of the viceroyalty, liberated section by section, with its capital at Bogota: Simon Bolivar became president and Francisco de Paula Santander vice president, under a constitution calling for a bicameral legislature. Gran Colombia matters because it was the boldest experiment of the independence era - the dream of holding the liberated north together as one great nation.
para2: The experiment did not hold. Rivalry for public office and regional jealousies led to a rebellion in Venezuela in 1826; after ruling as dictator from 1828 to 1830, Bolivar convoked a convention that produced a new constitution, but it was recognized only in Nueva Granada - Colombia and Panama - as Venezuela and Ecuador went their own way. Bolivar resigned and left for the northern coast, where he died, his uniform decorated with the medals of his campaigns: the Order of the Liberators of Venezuela, the Cross of Boyaca, and the Liberators of Cundinamarca. Gran Colombia dissolved in 1830, its member territories becoming the separate nations that stand today. Its short life left a lasting question for the continent: unity or fragmentation - a question the new republics answered differently, one by one.

title: The Empire of Brazil
titleline: The Empire of Brazil - The History Web
para1: The Empire of Brazil. The Empire of Brazil was born from a royal family in exile: when the Portuguese court crossed the Atlantic, Brazilians welcomed Dom Joao, who promptly abolished the Portuguese commercial monopoly on Brazilian trade and opened the colony's ports. But antagonism grew between Portuguese and Brazilians, republican propagandists gained influence, and when the Cortes demanded the young prince Pedro return to Portugal, most Brazilians supported his decision to stay. In January 1822 he formed a ministry headed by Jose Bonifacio de Andrada e Silva - a distinguished Paulista scholar later known as the Patriarch of Independence - and on September 7, on the plain of Ipiranga near Sao Paulo, he proclaimed the independence of Brazil. Portugal acknowledged it in 1825. The Empire matters because it gave South America's largest nation a strikingly orderly independence: a monarchy, not a republic, for nearly seven decades.
para2: Pedro I's popularity declined after he lost the Cisplatine province - now Uruguay - in a costly war, and under pressure he formally abdicated in 1831, leaving a child emperor and years of regency: from 1831 to 1835 a triple regency tried in vain to end civil warfare in the provinces. Under Pedro II, crowned young, Brazil found stability: relations with the United States and Europe were generally cordial, and the emperor himself visited Europe in 1871, 1876, and 1888. The era was marked by the bloody Paraguayan War - the War of the Triple Alliance of 1864-70, in which Brazil, allied with Argentina and Uruguay, prevailed - and by the slow death of slavery: the slave trade, promised away in 1831, did not completely cease for another twenty years, antislavery agitation began in the 1860s, and in 1871 Brazil enacted the Law of the Free Womb on the long road to abolition.

title: The Spanish American Wars of Independence
titleline: The Spanish American Wars of Independence - The History Web
para1: The Spanish-American Wars of Independence. The Spanish-American Wars of Independence had their harbinger in the Andes: on November 4, 1780, Tupac Amaru II - a kuraka of royal Inca blood - rose against the corregidor Arriaga, claiming to act under orders from the Spanish crown, and days later decreed the abolition of slavery for Black people, the first such decree in Spanish America, before his rebellion was crushed. The wars proper began with a collapse at the center: when Napoleon seized Spain and the Central Junta dissolved in January 1810, new juntas appeared across Spanish America, from Caracas on April 19 onward. In Mexico the revolt took the form of rebellion under Miguel Hidalgo, captured and executed in 1811, though resistance outlived him. These wars matter because they broke three centuries of Spanish rule and made a dozen nations.
para2: The wars were won by two great converging campaigns. From the south, Jose de San Martin raised the Army of the Andes in Cuyo, led the audacious Crossing of the Andes into Chile, and triumphed at Chacabuco and Maipu, becoming the Liberator of Argentina, Chile, and Peru. From the north, Simon Bolivar freed Venezuela and New Granada, forming Gran Colombia. When the two liberators met behind closed doors at the Guayaquil conference on July 26-27, 1822, San Martin withdrew from the scene and Bolivar took over the task of fully liberating Peru. The end came high in the Andes: on December 9, 1824, at the Battle of Ayacucho, Bolivar's lieutenant Antonio Jose de Sucre defeated the royalist army, and Viceroy Jose de la Serna, wounded, surrendered - while Sucre's campaign continued through 1825 in Upper Peru. Spain's continental empire was finished.

title: The Viceroyalty of New Granada
titleline: The Viceroyalty of New Granada - The History Web
para1: The Viceroyalty of New Granada. The Viceroyalty of New Granada was one of the principal colonial administrative changes effected by the Bourbon monarchs of Spain - a viceroyalty first established in 1717, suppressed in 1723, and reestablished in 1739, taking in present-day Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Venezuela, with its capital at Santa Fe de Bogota. Its creation reflected the growing population and increasing commerce of northern South America, as the Bourbon crown reshaped an empire that had long been ruled from Lima. This viceroyalty matters because it drew the political map from which the modern nations of the north of the continent would emerge.
para2: New Granada sat within a hierarchical system of colonial government, with the Crown and the Council of the Indies at the top and, moving downward, the viceroy, the audiencias, mayors, and local councils - a system designed to extract wealth while keeping officials in check. The Council of the Indies made colonial and ecclesiastical appointments, fixed the geographical scope of expeditions, and heard appeal cases from the colonial audiencias. The viceroy had overall responsibility for his jurisdiction and resided in the viceregal capital, but could not pass local legislation - though he could serve as president of the audiencia in his capital - that being the responsibility of the individual audiencias, courts with jurisdiction over a particular city and its surrounding area. The audiencia is thus the prime example of Spain's general approach to colonial government - great faith put in legal codes, and officers rotated to ensure they could not be easily corrupted. It was in this ordered world of viceroys and judges that the independence generation of Bolivar and Santander would grow up.

title: The Viceroyalty of Peru
titleline: The Viceroyalty of Peru - The History Web
para1: The Viceroyalty of Peru. The Viceroyalty of Peru was established in 1542 as Spain's second viceroyalty in the Americas, and at its height it encompassed part or all of modern-day Venezuela, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Paraguay, Uruguay, and Argentina - nearly the whole of Spanish South America. Its capital was assigned to Lima, the coastal city founded by Pizarro in 1535. The viceroyalty was born from conquest: it was in Cajamarca that Atahualpa had agreed to fill a room - seventeen feet wide and eight feet high - with gold and silver as ransom for his freedom, a moment captured in the famous colonial image of the Inka asked what the Spaniard eats, and answering: gold, and Spanish colonial rule in the Andes was only consolidated with the execution of Tupac Amaru, the last ruler of the Neo-Inka state, a semi-autonomous faction that held out after the empire's fall. This viceroyalty matters because for two and a half centuries it was the administrative heart of Spain's South American empire.
para2: Peru was more than a machinery of extraction: a vibrant artistic culture emerged throughout the viceroyalty's major cities, each a hotbed of artistic activity - Lima, the old Inca capital of Cuzco, and Arequipa in present-day Peru, and Quito in present-day Ecuador - where indigenous, European, and African traditions met in painting, sculpture, and architecture. From its Andean silver to its viceregal court, Peru set the pattern of Spanish rule on the continent, until the Bourbon reforms of the 18th century carved New Granada and the Rio de la Plata from its flanks and the wars of independence brought the viceregal age to an end.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Colonial Government in the Spanish Empire

title: The Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata
titleline: The Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata - The History Web
para1: The Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata. The Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata was Spain's fourth and last American viceroyalty - after New Spain, Peru, and New Granada - established in 1776 with its capital at Buenos Aires and including the territory now comprising Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Bolivia. The decision to carve it out of the Viceroyalty of Peru resulted from King Charles III's desire to decentralize the administration of his vast South American empire - and from Spain's wish to curtail the contraband trade flowing between Portuguese Brazil and Buenos Aires. This viceroyalty matters because its creation reshaped the economy of the southern continent and redirected the wealth of the Andes: the silver of the Potosi mines, previously exported via Peru, was now sent through Buenos Aires, and an enormous demand grew for salted meat, especially in Cuba. Its first viceroy, Pedro de Ceballos, pushed the Portuguese back and organized the new government in Buenos Aires before being supplanted by another viceroy just a few months later.
para2: The new capital thrived, and its people grew in confidence. When the British invaded Buenos Aires in 1806 and again in 1807, the viceroy twice fled - and twice the Creole population of the city successfully fought off the invaders on its own. That experience gave the Creoles confidence in their ability to govern and defend themselves, and in 1810, in the May Revolution, they created a provisional junta and exiled the viceroy. The youngest of Spain's viceroyalties thus became the cradle of Argentine independence, and the territories it had gathered - the pampas, the Paraguayan heartland, and the silver highlands of Upper Peru - went their separate ways into nationhood.

title: The Cisplatine and Platine Wars
titleline: The Cisplatine and Platine Wars - The History Web
para1: The struggle for control of the Río de la Plata, the River Plate estuary that gave the region its name, produced a series of wars among Argentina, Brazil, and the newly independent nations of Uruguay and Paraguay in the decades after independence. The Río de la Plata was one of the great trading arteries of South America, funneling the wealth of the interior to Buenos Aires and Montevideo, and whoever controlled its banks and navigation held the keys to regional power. The first and defining conflict was the Cisplatine War of 1825-1828 between the Empire of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, as Argentina was then known.
para2: The war began when the Banda Oriental, the east bank of the Uruguay River that Brazil had annexed as its Cisplatine Province, rose in revolt. Thirty-three exiled patriots, the legendary Treinta y Tres Orientales, crossed from Buenos Aires in April 1825 and raised the flag of rebellion, soon supported by Argentine troops. The decisive land battle came at Ituzaingó in February 1827, where an Argentine-Oriental army defeated a larger Brazilian force. At sea, the Irish-born admiral William Brown led a scratch Argentine fleet that harassed Brazil's far stronger navy and challenged its blockade of the Río de la Plata.
para3: Neither side could win outright. Brazil's blockade strangled Buenos Aires's trade, while Argentina could not dislodge Brazilian power ashore, and both economies bled. British mediation, driven by London's interest in keeping the trade routes open, produced peace in 1828: the Cisplatine Province became the independent nation of Uruguay, a buffer state between the two giants. The outcome satisfied no one fully, and Uruguay's politics split into the Blancos and Colorados, parties backed by competing foreign patrons.
para4: The struggle continued for decades through proxy wars and interventions. The Argentine dictator Juan Manuel de Rosas dominated the Plate through the 1830s and 1840s, blockading Montevideo in the long Great War, while France and Britain repeatedly intervened to force open the rivers. Rosas was finally overthrown in 1852 at the Battle of Caseros by a coalition of Uruguayans, Brazilians, and Argentine rebels under Justo José de Urquiza. The Platinum Wars set the pattern of rivalry and intervention that culminated a decade later in the devastating War of the Triple Alliance.

title: The Paraguayan War
titleline: The Paraguayan War - The History Web
para1: The Paraguayan War, also called the War of the Triple Alliance, was the deadliest conflict in Latin American history, a catastrophe that destroyed much of a nation. It pitted Paraguay, under the dictator Francisco Solano López, against the Triple Alliance of Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay. The war's roots lay in the tangled politics of the Río de la Plata: when Brazil intervened in Uruguay's civil war in 1864 to install a friendly Colorado government, Solano López saw the regional balance collapsing and demanded Brazil withdraw. When it refused, Paraguay seized a Brazilian steamer and invaded the province of Mato Grosso.
para2: To strike at Uruguay and Argentina, López requested passage for his army across Argentina's Corrientes province. When President Bartolomé Mitre refused, Paraguay invaded anyway in 1865, turning Argentina into an enemy. In May 1865 Argentina, Brazil, and the new Colorado government of Uruguay signed the Treaty of the Triple Alliance, pledging to fight until López was overthrown. Paraguay, though landlocked and outnumbered perhaps ten to one, had one of the strongest armies in South America, hardened by decades of military buildup under López and his father.
para3: The war began with Paraguayan offensives, but the Alliance soon gained the upper hand. The Brazilian navy destroyed the Paraguayan fleet at the Battle of Riachuelo in June 1865, seizing control of the rivers. Allied armies invaded Paraguay, and in May 1866 at Tuyutí they shattered the main Paraguayan army in the largest battle in South American history. The long siege of the fortress of Humaitá consumed two more years before the allies broke through in 1868 and took the capital, Asunción. López retreated into the northern hills and fought a brutal guerrilla war, drafting children and old men, until Brazilian cavalry cornered and killed him at Cerro Corá on March 1, 1870.
para4: The cost was staggering. Paraguay lost perhaps half its population, some estimates run even higher, including the great majority of its adult men, and saw its industry dismantled and its territory stripped by Argentina and Brazil. The war left wounds that lasted generations, yet it also forged national identities: Paraguay remembers López ambivalently as both national martyr and ruinous gambler, while Brazil's victory discredited its monarchy and strengthened its army. The war's trauma fed directly into the Chaco War between Paraguay and Bolivia two generations later.

title: The War of the Pacific
titleline: The War of the Pacific - The History Web
para1: The War of the Pacific reshaped the map of South America's west coast, costing Bolivia its access to the sea and leaving bitterness that endures to this day. The conflict grew out of the nitrate boom in the Atacama Desert, the driest place on Earth, where vast deposits of sodium nitrate, essential for fertilizer and explosives, had become enormously valuable. The richest deposits lay in territory belonging to Bolivia and Peru, but the mining companies working them were largely Chilean and British, and a tangle of tax disputes and border treaties set the stage for war.
para2: The spark came in 1878 when Bolivia imposed a new tax on the Chilean-owned nitrate company at Antofagasta, violating an 1874 treaty. When the company refused to pay, Bolivia seized its assets, and in February 1879 Chilean troops occupied the port of Antofagasta. Bolivia declared war, and Peru, bound by a secret defensive alliance with Bolivia since 1873, was drawn in. Chile thus faced two allies, but it held the decisive advantage: naval power. After sinking the Peruvian warship Huáscar at the Battle of Angamos in October 1879, Chile controlled the sea and could move armies along the coast at will.
para3: Chilean forces invaded Peru's Tarapacá province, winning hard-fought battles at San Francisco and Tarapacá, and then stormed the fortress of Arica in June 1880 after the bloody Battle of Tacna destroyed the allied army. In January 1881 Chilean troops occupied Lima itself, looting the Peruvian capital, including its national library. Peru's resistance continued in the Andean highlands under General Andrés Avelino Cáceres until 1883, when the Treaty of Ancón ended the war: Peru ceded Tarapacá outright, and Chile occupied Tacna and Arica pending a plebiscite that was long delayed and never fairly resolved the dispute.
para4: Bolivia made peace with an armistice in 1884, confirmed by treaty in 1904, losing its entire coastline and becoming landlocked. The disputes outlasted the fighting: the Tacna-Arica question festered unsettled for decades, a standing quarrel between Chile and Peru. Bolivia, however, never accepted its landlocked fate, and the demand for a seacoast remained the fixed star of its national politics. Chile gained the nitrate wealth that financed its golden age, while Peru suffered economic ruin and political collapse. The war redrew borders that remain fixed, but the grievances it created remain part of all three nations' politics.

title: The Jesuit Missions of Paraguay
titleline: The Jesuit Missions of Paraguay - The History Web
para1: In the subtropical forests where Paraguay, Argentina, and Brazil now meet, Jesuit missionaries and the Guaraní people built one of the most unusual experiments in colonial history: a network of mission towns, called reductions, that sheltered Indigenous communities from slave raiders and settlers for a century and a half. The first missions were founded in 1609 with the permission of the Spanish crown, which hoped the Jesuits would convert and pacify the frontier peoples at little cost. The Guaraní, skilled farmers who grew maize, manioc, and yerba mate, came to the missions partly by choice, fleeing the slave raids of the bandeirantes, the brutal slave-hunting expeditions from Portuguese Brazil.
para2: At their height in the early eighteenth century, thirty missions housed over one hundred thousand Guaraní. Each reduction was laid out around a vast plaza with a stone church, workshops, a college, and rows of family houses. The Jesuits governed in partnership with Guaraní chiefs, organizing communal agriculture, cattle ranches, and craft industries that produced everything from textiles to printed books. The missions became famous for their music: European instruments and polyphonic choral music took root, and Guaraní musicians composed and performed baroque works, a fusion that produced one of the most remarkable musical traditions of the colonial world.
para3: The reductions lived under constant threat. Bandeirante raids in the 1620s-1630s destroyed missions and carried off thousands of captives, forcing the Jesuits to relocate entire populations downriver. The crown then took the unusual step of arming the Guaraní, and mission militias defeated the bandeirantes in battle in 1641, securing the region. For generations the missions prospered, but they faced growing hostility from Spanish settlers and officials who resented Jesuit control of Indigenous labor and suspected the order of building a state within the state.
para4: The end came with the suppression of the Jesuits. In 1750 Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Madrid, redrawing borders and ordering seven missions east of the Uruguay River handed to Portugal, provoking the Guaraní War of 1754-1756 when the mission peoples refused to abandon their homes. Then in 1767 King Charles III expelled the Jesuits from all Spanish territories. Without their protectors, the missions declined: administrators looted them, residents drifted away, and the towns were abandoned to the forest. The ruins of San Ignacio Miní and Trinidad, now UNESCO World Heritage sites, preserve the grandeur of this vanished world.

title: The Rebellion of Tupac Amaru II
titleline: The Rebellion of Tupac Amaru II - The History Web
para1: In 1780 the viceroyalty of Peru exploded in the largest Indigenous uprising in colonial American history. Its leader, Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui, was a well-off cacique, a hereditary Indigenous chief, of the town of Tungasuca, who claimed descent from the last Inca and took the name Tupac Amaru II. The grievances were real and widely shared. The Bourbon monarchy had raised taxes and tightened colonial control, while local officials called corregidores forced Indigenous communities to buy unwanted goods at inflated prices through the repartimiento system, and men were still dragged away to the deadly mines of Potosi under the mita.
para2: The rebellion began in November 1780, when Tupac Amaru seized the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga, tried him before the community, and had him hanged at Tinta. He then proclaimed a program that mixed loyalty to the king with demands to end the repartimiento and the abuses of the mita, and he called on Indigenous people, mestizos, and even creoles to join him. Tens of thousands responded. His forces defeated a royal army at Sangarara and in January 1781 briefly besieged Cuzco itself, but they failed to take the city, and the colonial government rallied creole support by portraying the rising as a war of races.
para3: Royal forces captured Tupac Amaru in 1781, after the failed siege. On 18 May, in the main square of Cuzco, the Spanish authorities forced him to watch the execution of his wife and closest followers before putting him to death by quartering, a punishment meant to erase his movement from memory. The rebellion did not die with him. His kinsman Diego Cristobal Tupac Amaru fought on, and in Upper Peru, present-day Bolivia, the Aymara rose under Tomas Katari, who was killed in January 1781, and then under Julian Apaza, called Tupac Katari, who twice besieged La Paz in 1781 with an army of tens of thousands before he too was defeated and executed.
para4: By 1783 the last rebels had accepted amnesty or been crushed, at a cost of perhaps one hundred thousand lives. The crown responded with limited reforms, abolishing the corregidores and the repartimiento, but it also suppressed the Inca nobility's privileges and banned images and memories of the Inca past. The uprising was never forgotten. Rebels, reformers, and later independence movements invoked Tupac Amaru's name, and by the early twentieth century he had become a symbol of Indigenous dignity and resistance across the Andes.

title: Brazil's First Republic
titleline: Brazil's First Republic - The History Web
para1: On 15 November 1889 a military coup in Rio de Janeiro ended the Brazilian Empire without a fight. Emperor Pedro II, weary and isolated, boarded a ship for Europe, and Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca proclaimed a republic. The new order rested on an alliance of the army, the coffee planters of Sao Paulo, and urban enthusiasts of positivism, the philosophy whose motto, Order and Progress, still decorates the Brazilian flag. A constituent congress produced the constitution of 1891, which created a decentralized federal republic, separated church and state, and gave broad power to the states.
para2: In practice, power belonged to the states and their oligarchies. Politics ran on what Brazilians called coronelismo: local bosses, the colonels, controlled the votes of their rural clients in exchange for favors and protection. At the national level, the two strongest states, Sao Paulo and Minas Gerais, used their weight to place their candidates in the presidency more often than not, an understanding nicknamed coffee-with-milk politics. Elections were open affairs marked by fraud; the franchise formally excluded women and the illiterate, and corruption plus local intimidation kept most of the poor from voting, so the vast majority of Brazilians had no political voice.
para3: The economy of the republic was built on coffee and booms. The early years brought the Encilhamento, a speculative mania of banknotes and bubbles that burst in 1891. Coffee, led by Sao Paulo, expanded relentlessly, supported after 1906 by valorization schemes in which the government bought and stored surplus beans to defend the price. For a generation, wild rubber from the Amazon made Manaus one of the richest cities in the tropics, until Asian plantations destroyed the trade after 1910. Railways, ports, and European immigration, above all to the coffee fields of Sao Paulo, completed the picture of a country racing to modernize its export economy.
para4: The republic's apparent calm concealed chronic revolt. The navy rose against the government in 1893, monarchist rebels fought in the south, and the army destroyed the backlands community of Canudos in 1897. In 1904 Rio's poor rioted against a forced vaccination campaign. When the First World War came, Brazil joined the Allies in 1917 after German submarines sank its ships. The postwar years brought coffee crises, labor unrest, and a new threat from within the army: young lieutenants, the tenentes, rose in revolt in 1922 and again in 1924, seizing Sao Paulo for three weeks. By 1924 the First Republic's oligarchic system was visibly breaking down.

title: Suriname's Plantation Economy and Maroon Societies
titleline: Suriname's Plantation Economy and Maroon Societies - The History Web
para1: Suriname became a Dutch colony in 1667, when Dutch forces seized it from the English and the Treaty of Breda confirmed the conquest, just as it left the Dutch former colony of New Netherland in English hands. On the coastal plain the Dutch built one of the harshest plantation regimes in the Americas. Sugar, and later coffee and cacao, were produced by enslaved Africans who outnumbered Europeans ten to one, and the colony was notorious for its brutality. Paramaribo grew into a cosmopolitan port, home also to one of the oldest Jewish communities in the Americas, whose plantations at Jodensavanne lined the Suriname River.
para2: From the beginning, the enslaved resisted by running away. Escapees fled into the vast rainforest of the interior, where they founded independent communities that the Dutch could not destroy. Over generations these Maroons organized themselves into distinct nations, among them the Saramaka, the Ndyuka, and the Matawai, each with its own territory along the great rivers. They fought the colony's armies to a standstill, and in the 1760s the colonial authorities were forced to sign peace treaties recognizing their freedom: with the Ndyuka in 1760, the Saramaka in 1762, and the Matawai in 1767. In return, the Maroon nations promised to return future runaways, a clause that sat uneasily beside their own origins.
para3: The Maroon nations developed rich cultures of their own. Governed by paramount chiefs called granman, with councils, shrines, and their own languages blending African and European elements, they lived by farming, hunting, fishing, and trade with the coast. Their woodcarving, textiles, and oral traditions preserved African memories in new American forms, and their knowledge of the forest made them nearly unconquerable. Later groups, like the Aluku, won recognition after further wars, while Moravian missionaries gradually opened contact between the interior peoples and the colonial world.
para4: The coastal plantation system, meanwhile, went into decline. The Dutch abolished slavery in Suriname in 1863, but forced the freed people into ten more years of state-supervised labor, until 1873. To replace them the colony imported indentured workers from British India after 1873 and from Java after 1890, creating the remarkably mixed society of modern Suriname. In the early twentieth century the economy found a new base when bauxite mining began during the First World War. By 1924 the old sugar order was a memory, but the Maroon nations of the interior, treaty-bound and self-governing, remained the proudest survivors of the plantation age.

source3label: Duke University Press - Ethnohistory - via DOI

title: Argentina's Federalists, Unitarians and Juan Manuel de Rosas
titleline: Argentina's Federalists, Unitarians and Juan Manuel de Rosas - The History Web
para1: After independence from Spain in 1816, the United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata fell into a generation of civil war. At the heart of the conflict stood two visions of the nation. The Unitarians, based in Buenos Aires, wanted a centralized state modeled on European liberalism, with free trade and a strong capital. The Federalists, championed by the caudillos, the provincial strongmen who commanded the loyalty of the gaucho cavalry, defended provincial autonomy and traditional rural society. Between them, the provinces fought, united, and fell apart again, while Buenos Aires grew rich on the customs duties of the port.
para2: Out of this chaos rose Juan Manuel de Rosas. A wealthy rancher from Buenos Aires province and a master of gaucho cavalry, Rosas became governor in 1829. He stepped down in 1832 to lead a military campaign against the Indigenous peoples of the southern frontier, then returned to power in 1835 with sweeping authority. For seventeen years he ruled Buenos Aires and dominated the loose Argentine Confederation, a league of provinces without a national constitution, which the Federal Pact of 1831 had created. The other provinces kept their own caudillos, but Rosas controlled foreign policy, war, and the all-important customs revenue.
para3: Rosas governed through a mixture of popular support, patronage, and terror. He built a formidable following among the rural poor, Afro-Argentines, and the militia, while his supporters in the Mazorca, his enforcement organization, hunted down opponents, and public ritual demanded loyalty to the federalist cause, down to the obligatory red ribbon. Exiled Unitarians, including the writer Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, denounced him from Chile and Uruguay in works like Sarmiento's Facundo, which painted the struggle as one between civilization and barbarism. Foreign powers intervened too: France blockaded Buenos Aires from 1838 to 1840, and an Anglo-French fleet tried to force open the rivers between 1845 and 1850, but Rosas outlasted them both.
para4: The end came from within the federalist camp. Justo Jose de Urquiza, the caudillo of Entre Rios, broke with Rosas over control of trade and power, allied with Brazil and Uruguay, and defeated him at the battle of Caseros in February 1852. Rosas fled to exile in England, where he lived quietly as a farmer until his death. The victors gave Argentina a constitution in 1853 and, after a final decade of division, a unified national state in 1862. Rosas remained the most controversial figure in Argentine history: tyrant to his enemies, defender of national sovereignty against foreign intervention to his admirers, and inescapable to anyone explaining how the nation was made.

title: Argentina's Conquest of the Desert
titleline: Argentina's Conquest of the Desert - The History Web
para1: Through most of the nineteenth century, the pampas south of Buenos Aires remained Indigenous land. Mapuche, Ranquel, and Tehuelche peoples controlled the plains and hunted wild cattle, and their mounted raiding parties, the malones, periodically struck the frontier settlements, carrying off livestock and captives. Argentine governments built fort lines and signed treaties, but the frontier crept forward only slowly. By the 1870s the pressure became unbearable: the export economy needed the land for sheep and wheat, and landowners demanded that the state clear the pampas once and for all.
para2: The instrument of conquest was Julio Argentino Roca, minister of war and then president. In 1878 he launched the campaign remembered as the Conquest of the Desert. Five army columns advanced methodically into the pampas, and in 1879 they swept south to the Rio Negro, breaking the military power of the Indigenous confederations. Follow-up expeditions in the 1880s pushed into Neuquen and Patagonia. Thousands of Indigenous people were killed, and thousands more taken prisoner; families were divided, and captives were distributed as servants and laborers in Buenos Aires and the provinces or confined on islands and in camps.
para3: The conquered territory, an expanse larger than many European countries, was distributed with stunning speed. The state granted enormous tracts to officers, speculators, and land companies, laying the foundations of the great estates of Patagonia and the southern pampas. Sheep ranching spread over the grasslands, new towns and railway lines followed, and the newly won land fed the export boom that made Argentina rich. To the liberal elite, the campaign was a civilizing triumph that opened the desert to progress, and Roca rode its prestige to the presidency in 1880.
para4: For the Indigenous peoples, the conquest was a catastrophe from which recovery took generations. Survivors lost their lands, their mobility, and often their families, and were reduced to laborers on the estates carved from their own territory or pushed onto marginal lands. In the decades that followed, the official story taught in Argentine schools celebrated the campaign and largely erased its victims. Yet Indigenous communities in the south endured, and by the early twentieth century their descendants were beginning to organize and to challenge the story of an empty desert, a reckoning that was still only beginning in 1924.

title: Peru's Aristocratic Republic
titleline: Peru's Aristocratic Republic - The History Web
para1: Peru emerged shattered from the War of the Pacific (1879-1884), which had cost it its nitrate-rich southern provinces and left the state bankrupt and occupied. Recovery came under the Civilista Party, the party of Lima's merchants, planters, and bankers. In 1889 the government signed the Grace Contract, settling the foreign debt by handing the railways and vast guano and land concessions to the bondholders' Peruvian Corporation. In 1895 Nicolas de Pierola overthrew the military ruler Andres Avelino Caceres and inaugurated the Aristocratic Republic, two decades of rule by the coastal oligarchy.
para2: The Aristocratic Republic rested on exports and order. Sugar and cotton plantations on the coast, worked by wage laborers including Chinese and Japanese immigrants, supplied the world market. In the mountains, foreign capital returned to mining: in 1901 American investors founded the Cerro de Pasco Copper Corporation, which built smelters and railways and made copper a pillar of the economy. Lima was beautified with avenues and parks, and successive Civilista presidents managed the state in the interest of the forty families, as critics called the great fortunes who dominated finance, land, and politics. Elections were controlled, and the Indigenous majority of the highlands had neither vote nor voice.
para3: Beneath the surface calm, pressures accumulated. Workers on the sugar estates and in the mines organized and struck; an eight-hour-day movement swept Lima and Callao in 1913. President Guillermo Billinghurst, a populist millionaire elected in 1912, tried to court the workers and clash with congress, but the oligarchy and the army deposed him in 1914. The First World War first disrupted, then enriched the export economy. And in 1919 a new figure seized power: Augusto B. Leguia, a former president and businessman, who took office through a coup and began a new period of authoritarian rule.
para4: Leguia's early years promised modernization. With loans and contracts from American banks, he launched roads, irrigation, and public works, celebrated the centenary of independence in 1921, and patronized a new constitution in 1920. He also flirted with the new currents of the time: the university reform movement, the indigenista writers demanding justice for the highlands, and organized labor. But he ruled through repression, exiling opponents and muzzling the press, and his debt-fueled spending enriched a narrow circle. By 1924, when exiled students founded the APRA movement abroad, the oligarchic order the Aristocratic Republic had built was entering its final act.

title: British Guiana: Emancipation, Indenture and Plantation Society
titleline: British Guiana: Emancipation, Indenture and Plantation Society - The History Web
para1: British Guiana, on the northern shoulder of South America, was stitched together from the former Dutch colonies of Essequibo, Demerara, and Berbice, which Britain seized during the Napoleonic Wars and kept after 1815. It was a plantation colony built on sugar and on slavery. Behind great dikes that held back the sea and the rivers, estates produced sugar with the labor of enslaved Africans, whose suffering provoked one of the largest uprisings of the Caribbean: the Demerara rebellion of 1823, in which more than ten thousand enslaved people demanded their freedom and were answered with mass executions.
para2: Full emancipation came in 1838, after four years of a coerced apprenticeship that Britain imposed as a transition. The freed people moved quickly to build independent lives. Many left the estates and pooled their savings to buy abandoned plantations, founding free villages such as Victoria, purchased in 1839, which became centers of African-Guyanese farming, churches, and schools. The planters, facing the loss of their labor force, turned to a new solution: indentured immigration. Portuguese from Madeira came first, and Chinese laborers followed, but the great stream came from British India.
para3: Between 1838 and 1917, when the indenture system ended, nearly 240,000 Indians were brought to British Guiana under five-year contracts. They crossed the ocean packed in depot ships, were allotted to estates, and worked under penal laws that punished absence with prison. Wages were low, housing miserable, and protest dangerous: in 1905, colonial forces opened fire on workers at Ruimveldt during a dock and estate uprising. Yet the indentured endured, saved, and stayed. Most never returned to India; they re-indentured, bought small plots, planted rice, and built villages, temples, and mosques that transformed the colony's culture.
para4: By the early twentieth century British Guiana was a society of striking diversity held within a rigid colonial frame. Sugar, dominated by a few great firms like Bookers, still ruled the economy, though rice grown by small farmers was gaining ground, and bauxite mining began during the First World War. Political power rested with the planters and the Colonial Office, while a small educated class of African, Indian, Portuguese, and mixed descent pressed for reform. By 1924 the indenture era had closed, but its legacy, a multiracial population of Indigenous peoples, descendants of enslaved Africans, and families of Indian, Portuguese, and Chinese immigrants, defined the colony's future struggles.

title: Colombia's Thousand Days' War
titleline: Colombia's Thousand Days' War - The History Web
para1: The Thousand Days' War, which ravaged Colombia from 1899 to 1902, was the culmination of a century of conflict between Liberals and Conservatives. Under the constitution of 1886, written during Rafael Nunez's Regeneration, Colombia had become a highly centralized, church-allied republic in which the Conservative Party monopolized power and excluded the Liberals from office. The Liberals, strong among merchants, artisans, and coffee smallholders, chafed under discrimination, and when a crash in coffee prices ruined the economy in the late 1890s, revolution became their answer.
para2: The war began in October 1899 with Liberal uprisings in the coffee regions and along the Magdalena River. At first the rebels triumphed: in December their army won the battle of Peralonso, fought across a bridge in a two-day slaughter. The Liberal forces under Rafael Uribe Uribe then gambled on capturing the capital, but at Palonegro, near Bucaramanga, in May 1900, the Conservative army destroyed them in the bloodiest battle of the war. After Palonegro the conflict dissolved into years of guerrilla warfare, raids, and reprisals that burned through the countryside while the central government, beset by debts and intrigue, drifted.
para3: The human cost was staggering. Estimates commonly put the dead at around one hundred thousand or more, with disease and hunger adding to the battlefield losses. Property was destroyed, trade collapsed, and the paper money the government printed to pay for the war became worthless. The war also spread into Panama, then a Colombian province, where both sides fought for control of the railway and the isthmus while United States warships watched from offshore. In October 1902 Uribe Uribe surrendered at the Neerlandia farm, and the last rebels in Panama laid down their arms a month later aboard an American battleship.
para4: Colombia emerged from the war ruined and diminished. Exhausted and bankrupt, the government could not resist the secession of Panama in 1903, engineered with American support, and the loss of the isthmus became the war's most bitter legacy. Under the Conservative president Rafael Reyes, who ruled from 1904, the country slowly rebuilt its finances and railways, and the defeated Liberals reorganized as a legal opposition. Uribe Uribe himself, the great Liberal war leader, was assassinated in Bogota in 1914. The hatreds and the party banners of the Thousand Days' War, however, still defined Colombian political life in 1924.

title: Dutch Brazil and the Seventeenth-Century Atlantic
titleline: Dutch Brazil and the Seventeenth-Century Atlantic - The History Web
para1: In 1630 the Dutch West India Company seized Recife and the sugar captaincy of Pernambuco, beginning a quarter-century of Dutch rule in Brazil. The Netherlands, then fighting Spain for its independence, wanted the sugar and slaves of the South Atlantic, and Brazil, ruled by Spain's king since 1580, was the richest target. An earlier Dutch squadron had briefly taken Salvador in 1624. The conquest of 1630 proved more durable, and by 1641 Dutch control stretched along a thousand miles of the Brazilian coast from Maranhao to the Sao Francisco River.
para2: The golden age of Dutch Brazil came under Count Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen, governor from 1637 to 1644. He built a new capital, Mauritsstad, on islands beside Recife, with bridges, gardens, and palaces, and he governed with unusual religious tolerance for the era, allowing Catholics and Jews to worship openly. Recife's Jewish community built one of the first synagogues in the Americas. Johan Maurits also brought artists and scientists with him: Frans Post and Albert Eckhout painted the land and its peoples, while Georg Marcgraf and Willem Piso produced an influential early scientific study of Brazilian nature, the Historia Naturalis Brasiliae.
para3: Dutch power rested on sugar and the slave trade. The company kept the plantations running by compromising with Portuguese planters, and it seized Elmina in West Africa in 1637 and Luanda in 1641 to supply enslaved Africans. But the costs of empire mounted, the planters fell deep in debt, and many resented their Protestant rulers. After Johan Maurits was recalled in 1644, Luso-Brazilian landowners rose in revolt in 1645 under Joao Fernandes Vieira and Andre Vidal. Dutch attempts to hold the interior failed, and colonial forces, including units of Indigenous and Black soldiers, defeated company troops at the two battles of Guararapes in 1648 and 1649.
para4: Besieged in Recife, the Dutch surrendered in January 1654, and in 1661 the Treaty of The Hague confirmed the loss in exchange for compensation. The episode reshaped the Atlantic world. Dutch merchants carried Brazilian sugar techniques to the Caribbean, helping spark the sugar revolutions of Barbados and beyond, and Recife's Jews carried their community's memory to new homes from Amsterdam to North America. The paintings of Frans Post and the science of Marcgraf remained the most detailed European record of seventeenth-century Brazil, treasured long after Mauritsstad itself had vanished.

title: Chile's Parliamentary Republic and the Nitrate Economy
titleline: Chile's Parliamentary Republic and the Nitrate Economy - The History Web
para1: Chile emerged from the War of the Pacific (1879-1884) with a prize that transformed it: the nitrate deserts of Bolivia and Peru. The Atacama held the world's greatest deposits of sodium nitrate, the era's indispensable fertilizer and an ingredient of explosives. Foreign, mostly British, capital developed the oficinas, the desert processing plants, and nitrate taxes soon supplied half or more of the Chilean state's revenue. The new wealth made Chile the dominant power on the Pacific coast, but it also sharpened the struggle between president and congress over who would control the bonanza.
para2: That struggle exploded in 1891. President Jose Manuel Balmaceda, determined to spend nitrate revenue on railways, schools, and public works, defied a hostile congress, which declared him deposed. Civil war followed, and the congressional forces, backed by the navy and nitrate interests, crushed the presidential army in months; Balmaceda took his own life as his term ended. The victors built the Parliamentary Republic, an era from 1891 to the 1920s in which presidents were figureheads and cabinets rose and fell on votes of a fractious congress. Real power lay with shifting coalitions of Conservative, Liberal, and Radical bosses.
para3: The nitrate age created a new working class and a new social question. In the bleak desert pampa, tens of thousands of workers, the rotos of Chile and Peru and Bolivia, labored in brutal conditions, paid in tokens redeemable only at company stores. Their strikes were answered with troops: in 1907 the army massacred hundreds, perhaps thousands, of striking workers and their families at the Santa Maria School in Iquique, a wound the labor movement never forgot. Unions and mutual aid societies spread, and the Democratic Party and a growing workers' federation carried the miners' demands into politics.
para4: After the First World War, the system broke down. Competition from synthetic nitrate weakened demand for Chilean natural nitrate, and oficinas closed across the desert. Economic crisis met political paralysis: congress obstructed reform, and governments fell almost yearly. In 1920 the voters rallied behind Arturo Alessandri, the Lion of Tarapaca, who promised labor laws and social reform, but the old parliament strangled his program. In September 1924 young army officers, tired of the deadlock, rattled their sabres in the galleries of congress itself and forced reforms through; Alessandri left the country. The Parliamentary Republic was finished, and the age of military intervention had begun.

title: Palmares and Quilombo Resistance
titleline: Palmares and Quilombo Resistance - The History Web
para1: Throughout the seventeenth century, enslaved Africans in Brazil escaped the sugar plantations and built free communities in the forest. These settlements were called quilombos, and the greatest of them was Palmares, a confederation of villages hidden in the Serra da Barriga, in what is now the state of Alagoas. Founded around 1600, Palmares grew until it held thousands of people, with population estimates varying widely, organized in settlements called mocambos, protected by palisades, traps, and skilled warriors. Its people farmed, raised animals, traded with frontier towns, and raided the plantations, freeing captives and shaking the slave regime.
para2: Palmares was not a single tribe but a new African-American society. Its population came from many African peoples, joined by Indigenous allies and even poor settlers. At its head stood kings and war captains. The best remembered are Ganga Zumba, the great king who ruled from the capital village of Macaco, and his nephew Zumbi, born free in Palmares, educated for a time by missionaries, and destined to become the most famous quilombo leader of all. Portuguese and Dutch colonial authorities sent expedition after expedition into the forest, but the quilombo's warriors, masters of ambush and terrain, destroyed or outlasted them.
para3: In 1678, worn down by war, Ganga Zumba accepted a peace treaty with the governor of Pernambuco: the Palmarinos would keep their freedom but move to new land and return future runaways. Zumbi rejected any bargain that left others in slavery, and Palmares split. The king's peace collapsed, and by 1680 Zumbi led the war faction. For years he defied every army sent against him, becoming a byword for resistance along the whole coast. The colonists came to believe Palmares could only be broken by a massive, professional campaign.
para4: That campaign came in 1694, when the crown hired the feared frontiersman Domingos Jorge Velho, who stormed the fortified capital after a long siege. Zumbi escaped the fall of Macaco and fought on as a fugitive until November 1695, when he was betrayed, captured, and killed. The destruction of Palmares scattered its people. Quilombos continued to form wherever slavery existed in Brazil, keeping alive the practice of escape and independent settlement.

title: The Mapuche-Spanish Frontier and the Arauco War
titleline: The Mapuche-Spanish Frontier and the Arauco War - The History Web
para1: The Arauco War, the long struggle between the Spanish empire and the Mapuche people of south-central Chile, lasted nearly three centuries with periods of war alternating with diplomacy. The Mapuche had no kings or cities, but their decentralized communities, organized in local groups called lof and wider alliances, resisted Spanish conquest. When Pedro de Valdivia marched south in the 1540s and founded cities in Mapuche land, the toqui, or war leader, Lautaro studied Spanish cavalry and tactics, then turned them against the invaders. At Tucapel in 1553 the Mapuche destroyed Valdivia's force and killed him, and the war had begun.
para2: The decisive turning point came in 1598 at Curalaba, where Mapuche warriors killed the governor and sparked a general rising that destroyed seven Spanish cities south of the Biobio River. Spanish control contracted sharply. The Biobio became the main frontier zone, though Spanish enclaves survived farther south. On the Spanish side stood a costly line of forts and a permanent frontier army; on the Mapuche side, an independent land the Spanish called the Araucania, where war leaders were elected for campaigns and assemblies made decisions.
para3: War was only part of frontier life. From the seventeenth century, Spanish governors and Mapuche leaders held parlamentos, great treaty meetings that recognized Mapuche independence, regulated trade, and arranged the return of captives. Commerce in cattle, horses, ponchos, and salt flowed across the line, and so did people: settlers were captured and adopted, Mapuche worked on estates, and a mixed frontier culture emerged. Missionaries crossed in both peace and danger, while raids and reprisals periodically reignited open war. The Mapuche, meanwhile, spread their language and ways eastward across the Andes into the pampas.
para4: The frontier outlasted the Spanish empire. The new Chilean republic negotiated with Mapuche leaders, including at Tapihue in 1825, but as Chile grew stronger its settlers and governments pressed south. Beginning in 1861 under Cornelio Saavedra, and advancing decisively in the early 1880s, Chilean armies occupied the Araucania with forts, railways, and colonies. By 1883 organized resistance had been crushed and the Mapuche confined to small communal reserves. Into the 1920s they struggled to defend those remaining lands. Their long resistance remained central to Mapuche historical memory.

title: Venezuela's Caudillos and the Early Oil Economy
titleline: Venezuela's Caudillos and the Early Oil Economy - The History Web
para1: After independence, Venezuela spent a century ruled by caudillos, regional strongmen who rose by military force and governed through patronage. The most successful of the nineteenth century was Antonio Guzman Blanco, the Illustrious American, who dominated the country between 1870 and 1888. Guzman modernized Caracas with boulevards and monuments, built schools and telegraphs, and waged a fierce campaign against the Catholic Church, expelling orders and seizing its property. But his rule was personal and corrupt, and when he fell, the country dissolved again into rivalries among regional armies and ambitious generals.
para2: In 1899 a new strongman marched from the Andes: Cipriano Castro, who seized Caracas at the head of a private army. Castro's defiance of Venezuela's foreign creditors provoked a major international crisis. In 1902 Britain, Germany, and Italy blockaded and bombarded Venezuelan ports to force payment of debts, seizing or sinking much of the small navy. The crisis, resolved by arbitration in 1903, alarmed all of Latin America and prompted the Argentine jurist Luis Drago to declare that no power had the right to collect debts by force. The United States also asserted its own right to intervene in Caribbean states, a very different response to the debt question.
para3: Castro's own vice president, Juan Vicente Gomez, seized power in 1908 while Castro was abroad and remained the dominant ruler through 1924. Gomez, an Andean cattleman known as the Benemerito, ran the country like a private estate: he reduced public debt, crushed political rivals through a ruthless network of spies and prisons, and amassed one of the greatest personal fortunes in South America. Coffee and cacao exports funded the state, and the army and oil concessions went to his family and friends. Opposition existed mainly in exile, where critics plotted and wrote against the tyranny.
para4: Under Gomez, Venezuela's fate changed beneath the ground. Foreign companies, including Shell and subsidiaries of Standard Oil, won concessions and began drilling around Lake Maracaibo. A major commercial discovery came at Zumaque in 1914, and in December 1922 the Barroso Number Two well at Cabimas blew in as a spectacular gusher. The great oil boom had begun. By 1924 expanding oil production and foreign concessions were beginning to change the state's sources of revenue and its relationship with international companies. Coffee and cacao still mattered, but the political importance of petroleum was already clear.

title: The Abolition of Slavery in Brazil
titleline: The Abolition of Slavery in Brazil - The History Web
para1: Brazil imported more enslaved Africans than any other country in history, nearly five million people, and slavery reached into every corner of its economy and society. Yet between 1850 and 1888 the institution was dismantled step by step. The first great blow came against the slave trade itself. Britain pressed Brazil for decades to stop importing Africans, and in 1850, after British warships began seizing slave ships in Brazilian waters, the government of Eusebio de Queiros enforced a real ban. The transatlantic trade ended, and from then on the slave population could only shrink.
para2: Gradual emancipation laws followed. In 1871 the Law of the Free Womb declared that every child born to an enslaved mother was free, though such children still owed years of service to their mothers' owners. In 1885 the Sexagenarian Law freed enslaved people over sixty, a measure critics mocked as freeing those too old to work. Meanwhile an abolitionist movement grew into a mass crusade. The journalist Jose do Patrocinio, the statesman Joaquim Nabuco, the self-educated Black lawyer Luis Gama, and the engineer Andre Reboucas mobilized public opinion, while in the streets crowds blocked the recapture of runaways and whole provinces, like Ceara, freed their slaves ahead of the law.
para3: By the 1880s slavery was collapsing from below as well as from above. Thousands of enslaved people simply walked away from the plantations, hiding in quilombos and in the growing cities, and the police increasingly refused to hunt them. Planters, facing the loss of their labor force, began hiring European immigrants. In May 1888, with the emperor abroad, the regent Princess Isabel signed the Lei Aurea, the Golden Law, abolishing slavery completely and unconditionally. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery, and it did so without a civil war.
para4: Freedom came without land, compensation for the freed, or any plan for their inclusion, and the former slaves entered liberty with little more than the law on paper. Many continued to work the same estates for wages, while the coffee economy turned to European and later Japanese immigration. The abolitionist alliance with the monarchy also collapsed: the coffee planters, who blamed the crown for abolition, withdrew their support, and in November 1889 the empire fell. The Golden Law remained a source of pride, but by 1924 the descendants of the enslaved still faced the deep inequality that three and a half centuries of slavery had built.

title: Potosi, Silver Mining and the Colonial Mita
titleline: Potosi, Silver Mining and the Colonial Mita - The History Web
imagealt: A silver mine near Potosi, engraving from The Universal Magazine, c. 1750 (detail)
para1: Potosi lies at the foot of the Cerro Rico, the Rich Mountain, in what is now Bolivia, at about 4,067 meters above sea level. Diego Huallpa, an Indigenous prospector, is traditionally credited with discovering the Cerro Rico in 1545, and the town was founded the same year. Wikipedia says the mountain was the major supply of silver for the Spanish Empire until Guanajuato in Mexico surpassed it in the 18th century. It reports an estimate that the Cerro Rico produced about 60 percent of all the silver mined in the world in the second half of the 16th century.
para2: The wealth of Potosi rested on the mita, a Spanish system of forced labor based on an older Andean mit'a. Laborers came from an area of almost 200,000 square miles. About 13,000 men were conscripted each year, roughly one in seven adult Indigenous men. The mitayos faced harsh conditions, and carrying ore up from the mine to the surface in baskets, leather bags or cloth sacks was their task. Mercury was used to extract silver from poorer ores after the patio process was invented in 1554, and Wikipedia notes that mercury poisoning killed many people involved in refining.
para3: Potosi grew into a very large city. An anonymous description from 1603 counted some 6,000 Spaniards and other Europeans, 5,000 Africans, many people of mixed heritage and at least 120,000 native Andeans. Wikipedia reports that the population eventually exceeded 200,000. The city gave Spanish the expression valer un Potosi, 'to be worth a Potosi', meaning to be of great value. UNESCO says that in the 16th century the site was regarded as the world's largest industrial complex, with silver extraction relying on hydraulic mills supplied by aqueducts and artificial lakes.
para4: The city was also the site of the Spanish colonial silver mint, the Casa de la Moneda. UNESCO lists among its monuments the colonial town, the Church of San Lorenzo, patrician houses and the barrios mitayos, where the workers lived. During the Bolivian War of Independence, from 1809 to 1825, Potosi passed repeatedly between Royalist and Patriot control. The engraving on this page is a detail from a c. 1750 magazine print of a silver mine at Potosi. It is a contemporary European illustration, not a view of the mita at its height.
source2label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: City of Potosi
